authority: Cambridge Principal Examiner Reports for Teachers, 9702, March 2022 to November 2025, AS papers 11-13, 21-23 and 31-35 only. Each entry is a confusion the reports state candidates made.
derivation_policy: Curated by hand from the located error statements and restated in our words. No examiner-report wording appears in learner-facing output.
how_to_use: Every entry earns one MISCON card on its objective. A MISCON card is a DISCRIMINATION: the error, the correct idea, and the test that tells them apart (the test field). Multiple-choice distractors are built from these entries first.

kinds.adjacent_concept: Two different concepts that sit near each other in the syllabus.
kinds.near_neighbour_term: Two terms that share most of their wording or meaning.
kinds.wrong_angle_same_concept: The right concept answered from the wrong angle, or a step of it done wrongly.

entries.objective_text: recall the following SI base quantities and their units: mass (kg), length (m), time (s), current (A), temperature (K)
entries.a: Answering with base units (kg, A) or a derived quantity such as charge when base quantities are asked for
entries.b: The six AS base quantities are mass, length, time, current, temperature and amount of substance; kg, m, s, A, K and mol are their units
entries.test: Is each item in the answer a quantity or a unit?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /base (units|quantit)|coulomb.{0,25}base|units and quantities|SI units with SI base/

entries.objective_text: express derived units as products or quotients of the SI base units and use the derived units for quantities listed in this syllabus as appropriate
entries.a: Leaving a unit such as N, Pa or J in the answer when it must be written in base units
entries.b: A derived unit is rewritten as a product or quotient of kg, m, s, A, K and mol: N = kg m s⁻², Pa = kg m⁻¹ s⁻²
entries.test: Does the final unit contain base units only?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /base units|into base|cancelling of units/

entries.objective_text: assess the uncertainty in a derived quantity by simple addition of absolute or percentage uncertainties
entries.a: Adding absolute uncertainties for a product or quotient, or treating a percentage uncertainty as an absolute one
entries.b: Sums and differences: add the absolute uncertainties. Products and quotients: add the percentage (or fractional) uncertainties
entries.test: Is the derived quantity found by adding or subtracting, or by multiplying or dividing?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /percentage uncertaint.{0,50}absolute|absolute uncertaint.{0,50}percentage|confus\w+ .{0,30}uncertaint/

entries.objective_text: assess the uncertainty in a derived quantity by simple addition of absolute or percentage uncertainties
entries.a: Counting the percentage uncertainty of a squared or cubed quantity only once
entries.b: A quantity raised to the power n contributes n times its own percentage uncertainty: d³ contributes three times the percentage uncertainty in d
entries.test: What power does the measured quantity carry in the formula?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /double|factor of (two|three|2|3)|by three|by two/

entries.objective_text: understand the distinction between precision and accuracy
entries.a: Using precise and accurate as if they meant the same
entries.b: Accurate means close to the true value; precise means repeated readings agree closely with each other (small spread)
entries.test: Could a set of readings agree closely with each other and all be wrong?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /precis|accura/

entries.objective_text: understand and explain the effects of systematic errors (including zero errors) and random errors in measurements
entries.a: Believing that repeating readings and averaging removes a zero error or other systematic error
entries.b: Averaging reduces random error only. A systematic error moves every reading the same way and must be corrected at its source
entries.test: Does the error push every reading in the same direction?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /systematic|random error|zero error/

entries.objective_text: understand the difference between scalar and vector quantities and give examples of scalar and vector quantities included in the syllabus
entries.a: Calling work, energy, power, pressure or charge a vector
entries.b: Work, energy, power, pressure, charge, mass, speed and distance are scalars; force, displacement, velocity, acceleration and momentum are vectors
entries.test: Does reversing the direction change the quantity?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /vector|scalar/

entries.objective_text: represent a vector as two perpendicular components
entries.a: Swapping sine and cosine when resolving a vector
entries.b: The component alongside the angle is V cos θ; the component across from the angle is V sin θ
entries.test: Is the component next to the angle or opposite it?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /\bsin\b|\bcos\b|sinθ|cosθ|trigonometric/

entries.objective_text: recall and use the following prefixes and their symbols to indicate decimal submultiples or multiples of both base and derived units: pico (p), nano (n), micro (μ), milli (m), centi (c), deci (d), kilo (k), mega (M), giga (G), tera (T)
entries.a: Slipping a power of ten when converting a prefix (mA, µs, mm², GHz)
entries.b: Convert every value to base units before substituting; an area in mm² is multiplied by 10⁻⁶ to give m²
entries.test: Has every value been converted to base units first?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /power.of.ten|prefix|milliamp|picosecond|GHz|tera|giga|mm2/

entries.objective_text: define and use distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration
entries.a: Using distance where displacement is asked for, or speed where velocity is
entries.b: Displacement and velocity are vectors, so direction and sign count; distance and speed are scalars
entries.test: Did the object change direction during the motion?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /displacement|total distance|distance travelled/

entries.objective_text: determine acceleration using the gradient of a velocity–time graph
entries.a: Reading acceleration off a velocity–time graph as a value of velocity, or sketching velocity when acceleration is asked
entries.b: Acceleration is the gradient of the velocity–time graph; displacement is the area under it
entries.test: Is the question about the slope of the line or its height?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /gradient|velocity and acceleration|acceleration with velocity/

entries.objective_text: determine displacement from the area under a velocity–time graph
entries.a: Taking the area under a velocity–time graph as a triangle when the motion starts at a non-zero velocity
entries.b: The displacement is the whole area between the line and the time axis, including the rectangle under the starting velocity
entries.test: Does the line start from the origin?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /area under|trapezium|triangle/

entries.objective_text: solve problems using equations that represent uniformly accelerated motion in a straight line, including the motion of bodies falling in a uniform gravitational field without air resistance
entries.a: Assuming the start or end velocity is zero because the question does not state it
entries.b: Read u and v from the situation. At the top of a vertical throw the velocity is zero; at the top of a projectile path only the vertical component is
entries.test: Does the question actually say the object starts or ends at rest?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /initial velocity|final velocity|velocity of zero|was zero|at rest/

entries.objective_text: solve problems using equations that represent uniformly accelerated motion in a straight line, including the motion of bodies falling in a uniform gravitational field without air resistance
entries.a: Giving s, u, a and v inconsistent signs in vertical motion
entries.b: Choose one positive direction and give every vector its sign from it: with up positive, a = −9.81 m s⁻² throughout the flight
entries.test: Which way is positive, and do all four vectors follow that choice?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /\bsigns?\b|direction/

entries.objective_text: solve problems using equations that represent uniformly accelerated motion in a straight line, including the motion of bodies falling in a uniform gravitational field without air resistance
entries.a: Using speed = distance ÷ time for motion with a constant acceleration
entries.b: Distance ÷ time gives only the average speed; with constant acceleration use the equations of uniformly accelerated motion
entries.test: Is the velocity changing?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /constant (velocity|speed)|constant acceleration/

entries.objective_text: describe and explain motion due to a uniform velocity in one direction and a uniform acceleration in a perpendicular direction
entries.a: Using the whole launch velocity in vertical calculations, or adding the horizontal and vertical components as numbers
entries.b: Treat the two directions separately: vertically u sin θ with g; horizontally u cos θ, unchanged. Combine components only by Pythagoras
entries.test: Which component does gravity act on?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /component|horizontal|vertical/

entries.objective_text: recall F = ma and solve problems using it, understanding that acceleration and resultant force are always in the same direction
entries.a: Taking the resultant force to be one force alone (the tension, the weight, the driving force)
entries.b: F = ma needs the resultant force: combine every force on the object, with directions, before using it
entries.test: How many forces act on the object?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /resultant force/

entries.objective_text: state and apply each of Newton’s laws of motion
entries.a: Stating Newton’s second law as force equals mass times acceleration
entries.b: The second law links the resultant force to the rate of change of momentum: they are proportional and point the same way. F = ma is the special case for a constant mass
entries.test: Does the statement mention rate of change of momentum?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /second law|mass × acceleration|rate of change/

entries.objective_text: state and apply each of Newton’s laws of motion
entries.a: Treating the two forces of a Newton’s third law pair as acting on one object and balancing
entries.b: A third-law pair is equal in size, opposite in direction, of the same type, and acts on two different objects, so the pair never cancels
entries.test: Which object does each force act on?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /third law|action equals reaction|action.{0,10}reaction/

entries.objective_text: define and use linear momentum as the product of mass and velocity
entries.a: Subtracting sizes of momentum when an object bounces back
entries.b: Momentum is a vector. After a rebound the velocity changes sign, so the change m(v − u) is the sum of the two magnitudes
entries.test: Did the object reverse its direction?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /vector quantity|momentum.{0,40}(subtract|add|sign)|change in (speed|velocity)/

entries.objective_text: define and use force as rate of change of momentum
entries.a: Mixing up the change in momentum with the rate of change of momentum
entries.b: Δp is measured in N s; Δp ÷ Δt is the average resultant force, in N
entries.test: Has the answer been divided by a time?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /rate of change of momentum|change in momentum|p ?/ ?t/

entries.objective_text: describe and use the concept of weight as the effect of a gravitational field on a mass and recall that the weight of an object is equal to the product of its mass and the acceleration of free fall
entries.a: Mixing up mass and weight
entries.b: Mass (kg) is the property that resists a change in motion; weight (N) = mg, the pull of the gravitational field on that mass
entries.test: Is the answer in kilograms or in newtons?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /mass .{0,30}weight|weight .{0,30}mass|g = 9\.81/

entries.objective_text: understand that objects moving against a resistive force may reach a terminal (constant) velocity
entries.a: Saying that no force acts on an object at terminal velocity, or that drag rises while the object slows
entries.b: At terminal velocity the forces balance and the resultant is zero. Drag depends on speed, so it falls as the object slows
entries.test: Zero resultant force, or zero force?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /no resultant force|drag|terminal|resistive/

entries.objective_text: show a qualitative understanding of frictional forces and viscous/drag forces including air resistance (no treatment of the coefficients of friction and viscosity is required, and a simple model of drag force increasing as speed increases is sufficient)
entries.a: Drawing a drag or viscous force along the motion, or treating it as upthrust
entries.b: Drag and viscous forces act against the velocity and grow with speed; upthrust comes from a pressure difference in the fluid and acts upwards at any speed
entries.test: Does the force depend on how fast the object moves?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /viscous|drag force|upthrust/

entries.objective_text: state the principle of conservation of momentum
entries.a: Stating conservation of momentum without "total" or without the condition, or confusing it with the principle of moments
entries.b: The total momentum of a system stays constant provided no resultant external force acts on it
entries.test: Is the principle about turning (moments) or about motion (momentum)?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /isolated|closed system|momentum.{0,20}moment|moment.{0,20}momentum|total momentum/

entries.objective_text: recall that, for an elastic collision, total kinetic energy is conserved and the relative speed of approach is equal to the relative speed of separation
entries.a: Assuming kinetic energy is conserved in every collision
entries.b: Momentum is conserved in every collision; kinetic energy only in an elastic one, where the relative speed of approach also equals the relative speed of separation
entries.test: Is the collision stated to be elastic?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /kinetic energy|elastic|relative speed/

entries.objective_text: apply the principle of conservation of momentum to solve simple problems, including elastic and inelastic interactions between objects in both one and two dimensions (knowledge of the concept of coefficient of restitution is not required)
entries.a: Squaring the difference of the speeds, ½m(v − u)², to get the kinetic energy gained
entries.b: Square each speed first: ΔEk = ½mv² − ½mu²
entries.test: Is each speed squared before the subtraction?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /½m|\(v ?– ?u\)|v2\)|change in kinetic energy/

entries.objective_text: understand that the weight of an object may be taken as acting at a single point known as its centre of gravity
entries.a: Defining the centre of gravity as where the weight actually acts, or in terms of mass or gravity
entries.b: The whole weight of an object can be taken to act at one point, its centre of gravity
entries.test: Does the definition say the weight is taken to act there?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /centre of gravity|taken to act|actually acts/

entries.objective_text: define and apply the moment of a force
entries.a: Multiplying a force by a distance that is not perpendicular to it, or measured from the wrong point
entries.b: Moment = force × the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the force’s line of action
entries.test: Is the distance at right angles to the force and measured from the pivot?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /perpendicular distance|wrong distance|incorrect distance|distance to the|full length/

entries.objective_text: state and apply the principle of moments
entries.a: Stating the principle of moments without the sums, the common point or the equilibrium condition
entries.b: For a body in equilibrium, the total clockwise moment about any chosen point is equal to the total anticlockwise moment about that point
entries.test: Are the sums, the single point and equilibrium all in the statement?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /sum|same point|about a point|in equilibrium/

entries.objective_text: define and apply the torque of a couple
entries.a: Treating a couple as if it gives a resultant force, or using only half of the torque
entries.b: A couple is two equal and opposite parallel forces that are not in line: no resultant force, and torque = one force × the perpendicular distance between them
entries.test: Is there a resultant force?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /torque|couple/

entries.objective_text: understand that, when there is no resultant force and no resultant torque, a system is in equilibrium
entries.a: Concluding an object is in equilibrium because it is at rest, or from zero resultant force alone
entries.b: Equilibrium requires both zero resultant force and zero resultant torque
entries.test: Is the resultant torque zero as well?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /equilibrium because|stationary|resultant torque/

entries.objective_text: use a vector triangle to represent coplanar forces in equilibrium
entries.a: Labelling one side of the triangle of forces for a body in equilibrium as the resultant
entries.b: Forces in equilibrium form a closed triangle, so there is no resultant to label
entries.test: Does the triangle close?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /vector triangle|resultant force.{0,40}label|label/

entries.objective_text: define and use density
entries.a: Confusing the density of the object with the density of the fluid it sits in
entries.b: Density is mass per unit volume. In an upthrust problem the fluid’s density and the displaced volume go together
entries.test: Whose mass and whose volume are in the ratio?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /density/

entries.objective_text: calculate the upthrust acting on an object in a fluid using the equation F = ρgV (Archimedes’ principle)
entries.a: Using the object’s weight in place of the upthrust, or adding the upthrust to the weight
entries.b: Upthrust = ρ(fluid) g V(displaced), the weight of the fluid pushed aside; it acts upwards, against the weight
entries.test: Whose density and which volume go into ρgV?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /upthrust/

entries.objective_text: use the equation ∆p = ρg∆h
entries.a: Confusing pressure with force, or using a single pressure where the change in pressure is needed
entries.b: Pressure is force per unit area. Δp = ρgΔh gives the change between two depths, with Δh measured vertically
entries.test: Force or force per area; one pressure or a difference?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /pressure with force|pressure difference|change in pressure|single value of pressure|depth|height/

entries.objective_text: understand the concept of work, and recall and use work done = force × displacement in the direction of the force
entries.a: Using a force and a displacement that point in different directions, or the resultant force, to find work done
entries.b: Work done = the force × the displacement in the direction of that force
entries.test: Is the displacement along the line of the force?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /work done|direction of/

entries.objective_text: use the concept of efficiency to solve problems
entries.a: Putting the useful power where the total power belongs, or inverting the efficiency ratio
entries.b: Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input (both energies or both powers), so it is always less than 1
entries.test: Which is larger: what goes in or what comes out usefully?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /efficien|input power|output power/

entries.objective_text: define power as work done per unit time
entries.a: Treating power as the same as energy or work done
entries.b: Power is the rate of doing work: P = W ÷ t, in watts (joules per second)
entries.test: Has the energy been divided by a time?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /power (with|and) (the )?work|rate of work|power.{0,20}energy|energy.{0,20}power/

entries.objective_text: derive P = Fv and use it to solve problems
entries.a: Writing power as force divided by velocity
entries.b: P = W/t = F × (s/t) = Fv
entries.test: Does the unit come out in watts?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /P = F ?/ ?v|incorrect equation|symbol formula/

entries.objective_text: recall and use EK = ½mv²
entries.a: Forgetting to square the speed when substituting into Ek = ½mv²
entries.b: Square the speed before multiplying: v = 4.0 m s⁻¹ gives v² = 16 m² s⁻²
entries.test: Has the speed been squared?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /square/

entries.objective_text: recall and use the formula ∆EP = mg∆h for gravitational potential energy changes in a uniform gravitational field
entries.a: Using a height that is not the vertical change, or adding a change in height where it should be subtracted
entries.b: Δh is the vertical change in height. On a slope it is the distance along the slope × sin(angle to the horizontal)
entries.test: Is the height vertical, and is it a change?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /height|vertical component/

entries.objective_text: recall and use Hooke’s law
entries.a: Using the length of the spring or wire instead of its extension
entries.b: Extension = stretched length − original length, and F = kx uses the extension
entries.test: Has the original length been subtracted?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /length of the spring|total length|extension/

entries.objective_text: recall and use the formula for the spring constant k = F / x
entries.a: Adding spring constants for springs joined end to end
entries.b: Springs in series each carry the whole load, so their extensions add; springs side by side share the load, so their constants add
entries.test: Does each spring carry the full load?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /spring constants|single spring|composite/

entries.objective_text: define and use the terms stress, strain and the Young modulus
entries.a: Confusing stress with strain, or strain with strain energy
entries.b: Stress = F/A in Pa; strain = extension ÷ original length and has no unit; strain energy is the energy stored, in J
entries.test: Does the quantity have a unit, and which one?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /strain energy|strain with stress|stress with strain|confuse/

entries.objective_text: define and use the terms stress, strain and the Young modulus
entries.a: Defining strain without the word original
entries.b: Strain is extension divided by the original, unstretched length
entries.test: Which length is on the bottom of the fraction?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /original/

entries.objective_text: describe an experiment to determine the Young modulus of a metal in the form of a wire
entries.a: Converting a wire’s cross-sectional area from mm² wrongly, or using the diameter as the radius
entries.b: A = πd²/4 = πr², and 1 mm² = 1 × 10⁻⁶ m²
entries.test: Radius or diameter, and has the area been converted to m²?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /mm2|mm²|power-of-ten|diameter|radius|cross-sectional/

entries.objective_text: recall and use EP = ½Fx = ½kx² for a material deformed within its limit of proportionality
entries.a: Expecting double the extension to give double the stored energy
entries.b: E = ½kx², so doubling the extension multiplies the energy by four: the force doubles as well
entries.test: Does the force stay the same as the extension grows?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /double|quadruple|½kx|½Fx|E = ½/

entries.objective_text: understand and use the terms elastic deformation, plastic deformation and elastic limit
entries.a: Treating the limit of proportionality as if it were the elastic limit
entries.b: The limit of proportionality ends the straight-line region where F ∝ x; beyond the elastic limit the deformation becomes permanent (plastic)
entries.test: Is the question about the line going curved, or about the wire not returning?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /elastic limit|limit of proportionality|plastic/

entries.objective_text: understand and use the terms displacement, amplitude, phase difference, period, frequency, wavelength and speed
entries.a: Using displacement and amplitude as if they were the same
entries.b: Displacement is the distance from the rest position at one instant and changes all the time; amplitude is the largest displacement
entries.test: Does the quantity change from moment to moment?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /displacement|amplitude/

entries.objective_text: understand the use of the time-base and y-gain of a cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO) to determine frequency and amplitude
entries.a: Using the time-base setting as the period, or counting divisions for part of a cycle
entries.b: Period = the horizontal divisions for one complete cycle × the time-base setting (time per division)
entries.test: How many divisions does one whole cycle span?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /time-base|time base/

entries.objective_text: recall and use intensity = power/area and intensity ∝ (amplitude)2 for a progressive wave
entries.a: Assuming intensity is proportional to amplitude, or adding the intensities of two waves that superpose
entries.b: Intensity ∝ amplitude²; superposition adds displacements, and the intensity follows from the resultant amplitude
entries.test: Is the amplitude squared?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /intensit/

entries.objective_text: recall and use v = fλ
entries.a: Confusing the period with the frequency or the wavelength
entries.b: T = 1/f is a time; λ is a distance; v = fλ links them
entries.test: Is the answer a time, a distance or a rate?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /period|frequency|wavelength/

entries.objective_text: use the expression fo = fs v / (v ± vs) for the observed frequency when a source of sound waves moves relative to a stationary observer
entries.a: Swapping the source and observed frequencies, or the sign, in the moving-source formula
entries.b: A source moving towards the observer gives fo = fs v/(v − vs), higher than fs; moving away gives v + vs, lower
entries.test: Is the source approaching (pitch rises) or receding (pitch falls)?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /observed frequency|source frequency|doppler|speed of (the )?(sound|aircraft)/

entries.objective_text: recall the approximate range of wavelengths in free space of the principal regions of the electromagnetic spectrum from radio waves to γ-rays
entries.a: Naming the wrong region of the electromagnetic spectrum for a given wavelength
entries.b: In order of increasing wavelength: γ, X-ray, ultraviolet, visible (400–700 nm), infrared, microwave, radio
entries.test: What order of magnitude is the wavelength in metres?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /region|microwave|radio|ultraviolet|infrared/

entries.objective_text: recall and use Malus’s law (I = I0 cos²θ) to calculate the intensity of a plane-polarised electromagnetic wave after transmission through a polarising filter or a series of polarising filters (calculation of the effect of a polarising filter on the intensity of an unpolarised wave is not required)
entries.a: Using cos θ instead of cos²θ, or an angle that is not between the polarisation plane and the filter axis
entries.b: I = I0 cos²θ, where θ is the angle between the plane of polarisation and the transmission axis of the filter
entries.test: Is the cosine squared, and which angle is θ?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /cos2|cos²|cos ?\d|angle between|polaris/

entries.objective_text: compare transverse and longitudinal waves
entries.a: Classifying a sound wave as transverse, or expecting it to be polarised
entries.b: Only transverse waves can be polarised; sound in air is longitudinal, with oscillations along the direction of travel
entries.test: Are the oscillations along or across the direction the wave travels?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /transverse|longitudinal/

entries.objective_text: explain the formation of a stationary wave using a graphical method, and identify nodes and antinodes
entries.a: Explaining a stationary wave as two-source interference
entries.b: A stationary wave forms where two waves of the same frequency travel in opposite directions and superpose, often a wave and its reflection
entries.test: Are the two waves travelling towards each other?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /stationary|two-source interference/

entries.objective_text: understand how wavelength may be determined from the positions of nodes or antinodes of a stationary wave
entries.a: Taking the distance from a node to the next antinode as half a wavelength
entries.b: Neighbouring nodes are λ/2 apart; a node and the next antinode are λ/4 apart
entries.test: Node to node, or node to antinode?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /half (a|one|of one) wavelength|antinode|node/

entries.objective_text: explain the meaning of the term diffraction
entries.a: Describing diffraction as a wave bending when it enters a different medium
entries.b: Diffraction is the spreading of a wave as it passes through a gap or around an edge, in the same medium; bending at a boundary is refraction
entries.test: Does the wave change medium?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /refraction|diffraction|bending/

entries.objective_text: understand the terms interference and coherence
entries.a: Saying coherent waves have the same phase difference, or must be in phase
entries.b: Coherent sources have a constant phase difference between them (and so the same frequency)
entries.test: Must the phase difference be zero, or only unchanging?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /constant phase difference|same phase difference|in phase|zero phase/

entries.objective_text: recall and use λ = ax / D for double-slit interference using light
entries.a: Using the fringe spacing as the slit separation, or dividing a measured span by the number of fringes rather than the number of gaps
